rv.q: Anchuli Felicia King's Singapore-set drama brilliantly unpicks hypocrisy and the base values of the beauty business.
It’s a savage send-up of company culture that makes for incredibly exciting, excitingly stressful viewing, with a slick, tech-chic set (from Moi Tran) and vibrant characterisation.
King writes with brio and cleverly uses comedy to shock and to open up layers of prejudice and assumption.

Nana Dakin’s production is certainly over-broad at times, and has an occasional tendency towards shriekiness, but what King does so efficiently is to drive unflinchingly towards many awkward places it would be easier to swerve and avoid.
Yet WHITE PEARL as satire – the drama hinges on a racist ad that has gone viral – White Pearl is heavy-handed.
This turns out to be both its biggest strength and biggest flaw.
The actresses strut and stride, throwing back their heads and striking bodacious poses, but the dialogue, along with miserly plotting, makes for a cryptic challenge.
It looks good, but looks aren't everything, of course.
But putting the work in the studio upstairs would have signalled that the piece isn’t fully achieved yet.

The upshot of the furore soon begins to cause internal divisions in a company that is already riven with them, since it appears that every one of the women representing diverse Asian nationalities hates most, if not all, of the others.
It is mildly interesting, mildly well written and mildly amusing.
There’s substance to the satire of “White Pearl,” but its set-ups are so flimsy, it soon falls apart.
But the fact of the matter is that although it has wild energy, and is full of sharp and devastating observations, it doesn't quite land either as comedy or as satire.
This is a heartless, ill-plotted play by a writer who appears to loathe all the materials she has assembled: the characters, their jobs, their motives, their attitudes, and their use of language.

cn.t: King's debut satire about a Singapore cosmetics company's racist ad scandal offers sharp dialogue and vital Asian perspectives, but critics find the execution overly frenzied and the satire misfires more than it hits.
